unit.title: Perform internal and external customer service

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which of these is an internal customer of the firm's stores clerk?
options: An electrician who needs cable for a job
A home owner who phones for a quotation
The power company's meter reader on his rounds
A supplier's driver delivering breakers

questions.stem: Why does poor internal service, such as tools issued late from the store, affect the firm's clients?
options: It has no effect on the clients at all
It delays jobs and lowers what the client gets
It makes each client's final bill a lot smaller
It only affects the store's own paperwork

questions.stem: A client says, 'My breaker keeps tripping.' Which question helps most to find the cause?
options: Did you buy this house very recently?
Would you like a brand-new board fitted today?
Which breaker, and what is on when it trips?
Can you pay for the visit in cash today?

questions.stem: How should you explain to a home owner why their old wiring needs replacing?
options: Use trade terms, so that you sound expert
Say it is too complicated to explain to them
Scare them, so that they agree quickly
Use plain words, with the risks and choices

questions.stem: Why should the finish date you give a client allow for delivery times and the inspection?
options: So the date you promise is one you can keep
So the team can work more slowly on the job
So the client will pay the whole bill earlier
So the inspector can come on any day he likes

questions.stem: A client asks you to run his new A/C unit from an extension cord to save money. What should you do?
options: Do it, because the client is paying for the work
Refuse politely, explain the fire risk, offer a circuit
Do it, but say nothing about it to your supervisor
Use two extension cords so the load is shared

questions.stem: A client asks your team to 'just put in a bigger breaker' because a circuit keeps tripping. What is the best reply?
options: Fit the bigger breaker to keep the client happy
Fit a bigger breaker and ask them to watch it
Explain the cable limits the breaker; offer to find the fault
Tell them to use less electricity from now on

questions.stem: What is a 'service standard' in an electrical contracting firm?
options: The cable size that is used on most jobs
The fixed price charged for each service call made
The colour of uniform the staff must wear
A set target, such as calls returned in 4 hours

questions.stem: A client complains that the team left dust and offcuts in her house. As team leader, what should you do first?
options: Apologise, listen fully and arrange a clean-up
Tell her that her own cleaner will see to it later
Explain that dust is normal on every job
Ask her to write it down and then wait

questions.stem: After a complaint has been put right, why should the team leader find out why it happened?
options: So that someone in the team can be blamed
So the same problem does not happen again
So the client can be charged for the visit
So the complaint record can then be deleted

questions.stem: A client's complaint turns out to be a billing error that only the office can correct. What should you do?
options: Tell the client that it is not your job
Promise a refund that you cannot approve
Pass it on, and tell the client who and when
Ignore it until the client phones again

questions.stem: While a client describes a fault, what is the best way to show you have understood?
options: Start writing out the bill while they talk
Interrupt them to give your answer early
Look on your phone for a spare part that might fit
Repeat the main points back in your own words

questions.stem: At the end of a job, what should you show a home owner about their new distribution board?
options: How to use the main switch and reset a breaker
How to change the breakers by themselves
How to work on the board safely while it is live
How to take off the board's front cover

questions.stem: Why should a firm keep clients' alarm codes and keys in a locked, recorded place?
options: So any worker can visit the house when they like
To protect the clients' security and privacy
So the codes can be shared with other clients
So the keys are easy for staff to have copied

questions.stem: Why is a short report written after each service call?
options: So the van's mileage is recorded for the office
So the client has to sign the job card twice
So the next visit knows what was found and done
So the technician has something to do at the end

questions.stem: The stores clerk keeps getting unclear requests such as 'some cable'. As team leader, what is the best fix?
options: Tell the clerk to guess what each person needs
Let each electrician take their own stock
Stop using the store and buy from shops
Agree a request form with size, type and quantity

questions.stem: A client phones while you are on a roof finishing a fixing. What is the best action?
options: Finish the step safely, get down, then call back
Answer it while holding on to the roof with one hand
Ignore the call and never ring them back
Throw the phone down to a worker below

questions.stem: Which is the best way to find out whether clients are happy with the firm's service?
options: Count how many vans the firm has on the road
Ask each client a few short questions after the job
Ask only the firm's own staff what they think
Wait for complaints and treat silence as success

questions.stem: Feedback shows clients often were not told when the team would arrive. Which change would help most?
options: Arrive earlier than planned without telling them
Stop asking clients for feedback after jobs
Message each client the day before with a time
Give the team longer lunch breaks each day

questions.stem: A client is deaf and uses written notes. What is the best way to explain the job to her?
options: Speak louder and faster so she can follow
Explain it only to her next-door neighbour
Skip the explanation to save her time
Write clear notes, use sketches, check understanding

questions.stem: The plumber on site asks your team to move a cable that is in the way of a new pipe. What is the best response?
options: Agree a solution, and isolate safely if it must move
Tell the plumber it is not your team's problem at all
Let the plumber move your cable himself
Cut the cable so the pipe can pass through

questions.stem: Why should a team leader make sure the team's vans and uniforms are clean and tidy?
options: So the vans use less fuel on each trip
Clients judge the firm's care by what they see
So the team finishes each job a little bit faster
So fewer clients ask the firm for a quote

questions.stem: You told a client you would bring a part on Thursday, but it will not arrive until Monday. What should you do?
options: Say nothing, and simply go on Monday
Go on Thursday anyway without the part
Call before Thursday and agree a new date
Wait for the client to call you first

questions.stem: An angry client shouts at a trainee in your team on site. As team leader, what should you do?
options: Shout back to defend the trainee
Leave the trainee to deal with it alone
Pack up the tools and leave the site
Step in calmly, move somewhere quiet, listen

questions.stem: Why should a written quotation say what is NOT included, such as patching and painting walls?
options: So the client knows what to expect later
So the firm can charge more without saying
So the quotation looks longer and fuller
So the client is sure to pick another firm

questions.stem: Six weeks after a job, a GFCI outlet keeps tripping. The work has a 3-month warranty. What should the firm do?
options: Charge for a new outlet before visiting
Visit to find the cause; no charge if it is our fault
Tell the client to take the GFCI out
Say the warranty covers labour only

questions.stem: What is the best way to pass a client's special request to the team who will do the job?
options: Hope that somebody in the team remembers it
Ask the client to repeat it to each worker
Write it on the job card and brief the team
Mention it to them after the job is finished

questions.stem: A client's dog is loose in the yard where the team must work. What should you do?
options: Chase the dog out of the yard yourself
Work around the dog and hope it is calm
Leave the site and charge for the visit
Ask the client to secure the dog first

questions.stem: A client offers your team cash to do extra work 'off the books'. What should you do?
options: Decline, and refer the work to the firm
Accept, since the client is asking
Accept, and share the cash out evenly
Do the work, but give the client no receipt for it

questions.stem: A team arrived two hours late for a client in Spanish Town. Which response is best?
options: Blame the traffic and say nothing more
Apologise, explain briefly and do the job well
Say nothing, since they did arrive in the end
Charge the client extra for the waiting time

questions.stem: A client says she does not understand her invoice. What should you do?
options: Tell her to call the office later on
Say the amount is fixed and cannot be explained
Go through each line and answer her questions
Lower the price so that the questions stop

questions.stem: A visitor staying at a villa asks whether his equipment from abroad can be plugged into the outlets. What is the most useful advice?
options: Any equipment will work on any voltage
Plug it in and see what happens to it
Use any adapter that fits the outlet
Check its rated voltage before plugging in

questions.stem: Why should a team leader plan the day's service calls by area?
options: Less travel leaves more time for each client
So the team can stop at their own homes
So the van does not need any more fuel
So clients who live far away are never served

questions.stem: The office needs each job's timesheet by Friday to bill clients. Why should the team leader make sure it arrives on time?
options: So the office staff have less work to do
Late timesheets delay billing and cash flow
So the workers are paid less that week
So every client receives a small discount

questions.stem: A client posts a public complaint about the firm online. What is the best first step?
options: Reply angrily to defend the firm's name
Post the client's address for everyone to see
Reply politely and offer to talk privately
Ignore it completely and hope it goes away

questions.stem: Why should the team leader tell a shop owner which areas are unsafe while the team works?
options: So the owner can supervise the electricians
So the shop can close early for the day
So the team can work without isolating
So staff and shoppers keep out of danger

questions.stem: A client asks which LED lights to buy. What is the best way to advise her?
options: Explain choices, costs and savings; let her decide
Tell her to buy the most expensive ones in the shop
Say that all LED lights are exactly the same
Refuse to give any advice about products

questions.stem: Why does a firm write down how staff should answer calls, give quotes and follow up?
options: So staff do not need to think for themselves
So every client gets the same good service
So clients are not able to make complaints
So the office is able to close earlier

questions.stem: A new team member is often curt and rude with clients. What should the team leader do?
options: Shout at him in front of the client
Ignore it, as long as his work is good
Talk with him privately and coach him
Send him home at once without pay

questions.stem: A client changes her mind about outlet positions after first fix is done. What is the best response?
options: Refuse to change anything at all now
Change them and say nothing about cost
Say the inspector will not allow changes
Explain the cost and time; confirm in writing

questions.stem: A restaurant owner wants 'more light' in the dining room. What should you find out first?
options: The room's use, the mood wanted and the budget
The owner's favourite colour for the dining room walls
How many tables are booked for tonight
Which supplier the owner prefers to use

questions.stem: When a job is finished, who inside the firm needs the test results and job notes?
options: Nobody, because the client keeps them all
The office, for the job file and billing
The store clerk, and nobody else
The van driver, for the route sheet

questions.stem: A client's beliefs mean no work may be done in the house on Saturdays. What should you do?
options: Work on Saturday anyway to keep to time
Charge her extra for the lost working day
Respect it and plan the work for other days
Ask her to change her beliefs for the job

questions.stem: Which measure would best show that a team's service is getting better over a year?
options: More vans parked in the firm's yard
Longer jobs on average than in the year before
More staff working in the office
Fewer complaints and call-backs per job

questions.stem: A client is rushing you to finish before a party tonight, but the testing is not done. What should you do?
options: Explain it cannot be energised until tested
Skip the tests to meet the client's deadline
Energise it tonight and test it tomorrow
Leave the client to switch it on later

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What do we call a person inside your own firm who relies on your work, such as the stores clerk or the office?
What do we call the client or member of the public who pays for or uses the firm's services?
What is a return visit to put right a fault in work already done usually called?
What two-word term describes listening carefully, nodding and repeating back what was said?
A service standard says calls are returned within 4 hours. A call comes in at 10:30 a.m. By what time must it be returned?
Of 40 clients asked, 34 said they were satisfied. What percentage is that?
What word describes a client's statement that they are unhappy with the service?
What one word means the comments clients give about the service, good or bad?
What is the name for a call or visit made soon after a job to check that the client is happy?
What is it called when a problem is passed to a more senior person who can deal with it?
What kind of question, starting with words like 'what' or 'how', gets the client to explain in their own words?
A firm had 8 complaints from 200 jobs last year. What percentage of jobs had a complaint?
Which document sets out the work, price and terms offered to a client before the job is agreed?
What is the meeting called at the end of a job where the work and documents are explained to the client?
Which word describes the firm's duty not to share a client's alarm codes, keys or personal details?

essays.stem: Explain the difference between internal and external customers in an electrical contracting firm. Give two examples of each and say how each is served well.
essays.modelAnswer: External customers are people outside the firm who pay for or use our work, such as a home owner who wants a rewire, or a hotel manager who needs lighting repaired. They are served well by listening to their needs, giving clear prices and dates, doing safe, tidy work and following up. Internal customers are people inside the firm who depend on our work so they can do theirs. For example, the stores clerk needs clear, written requests from the electricians, and the office needs accurate timesheets, job notes and test results on time to bill the client. They are served well by giving them what they need, correctly and on time, and treating them with the same respect as clients. Good internal service makes good external service possible: if the store or office is let down, the client is let down too.
markingPoints: Defines external customers with two examples
How external customers are served well
Defines internal customers with two examples
How internal customers are served well
Links internal service to the service the client gets

essays.stem: Describe how you would find out a client's needs during a first visit to a home that needs more outlets and better lighting.
essays.modelAnswer: I would arrive on time, introduce myself and show my ID, and ask permission before walking round. I would ask open questions, such as 'How do you use this room?' and 'What problems do you have now?', and listen without interrupting. I would ask about the budget, the timing and any furniture or appliances planned. I would walk through each room with the client, noting where outlets and lights are wanted and checking the board and existing wiring. I would repeat the main points back to check I have understood, and write them down. If the client asks for something unsafe or against the code, I would explain why and offer a safe choice. Before leaving I would tell them what happens next, such as when they will get a written quotation, and thank them for their time.
markingPoints: Arrives on time, introduces self, asks permission
Uses open questions and listens
Asks about budget, timing and plans; walks each room and checks the installation
Repeats back and writes down the needs; deals with unsafe requests
Explains next steps and thanks the client

essays.stem: A client asks you to do something unsafe to save money. Explain how you would handle the conversation and keep the client's goodwill.
essays.modelAnswer: For example, a client may ask me to put a bigger breaker on a circuit that keeps tripping. I would stay calm and polite and show that I understand the problem and the wish to save money. I would explain, in plain words, why it is unsafe: the breaker protects the cable, and a bigger one would let the cable overheat and could start a fire. I would make it clear that I cannot do it because it would put the family at risk and break the rules the firm works to. Then I would offer safe choices: find out why it is tripping, move some load to another circuit, or add a new circuit, with a clear price for each. I would put my advice in writing. Most clients respect an electrician who protects them, and they trust the firm more.
markingPoints: Stays calm and polite and shows understanding
Explains the danger in plain words
Refuses clearly and gives the reason
Offers safe alternatives with prices
Records the advice and keeps the client's trust

essays.stem: Describe the steps you would follow, as team leader, to deal with a complaint about the team's work, from the first call to the follow-up.
essays.modelAnswer: I would thank the client for telling us and listen to the whole complaint without arguing or making excuses. I would ask questions to get the facts and repeat them back. I would apologise for the trouble and say what I will do and by when. I would record the complaint in the firm's log. I would visit or check the facts, and if there is any danger, make the installation safe at once. I would agree the fix with the client and arrange it quickly, done by a competent person. If it is something I cannot decide, such as a refund, I would pass it to the manager and tell the client who will contact them. When the fix is done, I would check it and call the client to make sure they are satisfied. Finally I would find the cause with the team and make changes so it does not happen again.
markingPoints: Listens, thanks and apologises without arguing
Gets the facts and records the complaint
Makes safe and agrees and carries out the fix promptly
Escalates what is beyond their authority and keeps the client informed
Follows up and removes the cause

essays.stem: Explain how you would explain a technical problem, such as a faulty earth, to a client who has no electrical knowledge.
essays.modelAnswer: I would choose a quiet moment and use plain, everyday words, not trade terms. I would explain what the earth does in a simple way: it is a safety path that carries a fault away so the breaker trips, and stops the metal case of an appliance becoming live. I would then say what we found, for example the earth wire to the kitchen outlets is broken, and what that means: if an appliance develops a fault, someone touching it could get a shock. I might use a simple sketch or show the faulty part. I would explain what needs to be done, how long it will take and what it will cost, and whether the circuit must stay off until it is fixed. I would invite questions and check they have understood by asking them to tell me what they will do next.
markingPoints: Uses plain words, no jargon
Explains what the earth does simply
Says what was found and what the risk is
Uses a sketch or shows the part; explains fix, time, cost and any need to keep it off
Invites questions and checks understanding

essays.stem: Describe how a team leader can improve the service the team gives to the office, the store and other trades on site.
essays.modelAnswer: A team leader should first ask each internal customer what they need from the team and what goes wrong now. For the office, the team can hand in complete timesheets, job notes, test results and variation forms on time, so jobs can be billed and certified. For the store, the team can use a clear request form with size, type and quantity, order in good time, return unused materials and report damaged tools. For other trades on site, the team can share its programme, keep to agreed times, keep its work area tidy, and agree routes for cables and pipes before work starts. If a cable must be moved, it is done safely by the team after isolation. The team leader should set simple standards, explain why they matter, check them and thank people who keep them. Problems should be talked through calmly and fixed.
markingPoints: Asks internal customers what they need
Office: complete paperwork on time
Store: clear requests, timely orders, returns
Other trades: share programme, keep times, tidy area, agree routes, safe changes
Sets standards, checks them and solves problems

essays.stem: Explain how you would collect and use client feedback to improve the firm's service.
essays.modelAnswer: I would collect feedback after every job using a few short questions, by phone, a message or a printed card. I would ask about arrival times, tidiness, how well things were explained, the quality of the work and whether the client would use us again, with space for comments. I would also record complaints, compliments and call-backs. Each month I would put the results together and look for patterns, such as many clients saying they were not told when the team would arrive. I would discuss the results with the team and the manager, choose one or two improvements, such as sending a message the day before each visit, and put them into practice. Then I would watch the next months' feedback to see if the change worked. I would also thank clients for their feedback and reply to any who raised a problem.
markingPoints: Collects feedback after each job with short questions
Also records complaints, compliments and call-backs
Looks for patterns regularly
Agrees and makes improvements with the team and manager
Checks the effect and responds to clients

essays.stem: Describe what you would explain and hand over to a client at the end of an installation job.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would make sure the work is finished, tested, passed and the area cleaned, and that the instructor or authorised person has energised it. I would walk the client round and show what was done. I would show the main switch and how to switch off in an emergency, how to reset a tripped breaker, and how to press the test button on GFCI outlets regularly. I would explain any new equipment, such as a timer or isolator, and warn them not to overload circuits or use unsafe adapters. I would hand over the test results or certificate, the updated circuit chart, the makers' manuals and warranties, and the invoice. I would explain our warranty and how to contact us. I would answer questions, ask the client to sign that they have received everything, and thank them for their business.
markingPoints: Work finished, tested, passed, cleaned and energised by the authorised person
Shows main switch, breaker reset and GFCI test
Explains new equipment and safe use
Hands over test results, circuit chart, manuals, warranties and invoice
Explains warranty and contact; signed acceptance; thanks the client

essays.stem: Explain how you would serve clients of different backgrounds, ages and abilities fairly and with respect. Give examples.
essays.modelAnswer: Every client should get the same standard of service, whatever their age, background, religion, gender, disability or how much money they have. I would be polite, patient and listen to each person. I would change the way I communicate to suit the person, not the quality of the service. For example, for an elderly client I would speak clearly, give them time and write down the key points. For a deaf client I would use written notes and sketches. For a client in a wheelchair I would make sure they can reach the switches and controls we fit. For a visitor who speaks little English or uses different words, I would use simple words and check understanding. I would respect cultural or religious needs, such as not working on certain days. I would never make jokes or comments about anyone's background.
markingPoints: Same standard of service for everyone
Polite, patient and listens
Adapts communication to the person
Gives at least two suitable examples
Respects cultural or religious needs; no jokes or comments

essays.stem: Explain why keeping promises on times and prices matters in customer service, and what to do when a promise cannot be kept.
essays.modelAnswer: When we keep our promises, clients trust us, recommend us and come back. A client may have taken time off work, arranged for a building to be empty, or planned money around our price, so a broken promise costs them time and money and damages the firm's name. To keep promises, I would only promise dates and prices I am confident of, allowing for delivery times and the inspection, and write them down. If something changes and a promise cannot be kept, I would tell the client as early as possible, not wait for them to find out. I would apologise, explain the reason honestly, and give a new date or price with the reason in writing. Where possible I would offer something to reduce the trouble, such as doing part of the work first. Then I would make sure the new promise is kept.
markingPoints: Kept promises build trust and repeat business
Broken promises cost the client time and money and harm the firm
Only promises realistic dates and prices, in writing
Tells the client early, apologises and explains honestly
Gives a new date or price in writing, reduces the trouble, then keeps it

practical1.title: Role play: first visit, client needs record and written job proposal
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group three client cards: a home owner in Portmore who wants more outlets and better lighting, a restaurant owner whose breakers keep tripping, and a villa manager whose guests need help with the supply for their equipment. One card includes an unsafe request. For each card, one member plays the electrician or team leader, one plays the client (using the card), and the others observe with a checklist. Then the roles rotate so that every member leads at least one visit. In each visit the 'electrician' greets the client, asks open questions, repeats back the needs, deals politely with any unsafe request and explains the next steps. After each visit, the pair writes a needs record and a short job proposal in plain words: the work, the safety points, the time, the price before GCT and a GCT line at the rate the assessor gives, and what is not included. The observers give written feedback. Photograph each stage and hand in all records.
materials: Needs record forms, job proposal forms and observer checklists
Price list and GCT rate from the assessor
Floor plan sketches for each client, pens and calculators
Table and chairs set out as a client's room or office
photos: The role-play set-up with the client card
The observer checklist being filled in
The written job proposal with GCT shown
checklist: Greeted the client politely and introduced themselves
Asked open questions and listened without interrupting
Repeated the client's needs back and recorded them accurately
Refused any unsafe request politely and offered a safe choice
Wrote a clear job proposal in plain words, with a correct price and GCT line
Gave useful written feedback as an observer
Explained the next steps and thanked the client
safety: This is a role play: no tools or supplies are used
Treat each other with respect during the role play and the feedback
Do not give real clients' names or addresses on any form
Keep the room tidy and walkways clear

practical2.title: Handle a complaint and set up service standards for internal and external customers
practical2.brief: Part A: the assessor plays an unhappy client who complains that a new outlet circuit keeps tripping and that the team left a mess. One member acts as team leader and handles the complaint; one acts as the trainee who did the work; the others observe. Roles rotate so that every member handles a complaint (the assessor changes the details each time). Each complaint is entered in a complaint log with the facts, the agreed fix, any escalation and the follow-up date. Part B: as a group, write (1) three service standards for external clients, such as call-back times; (2) a simple internal request form for the store, with size, type and quantity; (3) a five-question client feedback card; and (4) a poster for the workshop wall that shows the steps for handling a complaint. Test the request form by role-playing an electrician and the stores clerk. Each member leads one item in Part B. Photograph each stage and hand in the log, forms and poster.
materials: Complaint log sheets and observer checklists
Flip-chart paper, markers and coloured pens for the poster
Paper or a computer for the forms and the feedback card
photos: A complaint being handled in the role play
The internal request form being tested with the stores clerk
checklist: Stayed calm, listened fully and apologised without arguing
Got the facts, agreed a clear fix and gave a time
Escalated what was beyond their authority and told the client who would act
Recorded the complaint accurately in the log
Led one Part B item and made it clear and usable
Took part in testing the internal request form
safety: This is a role play and desk task: no tools or supplies are used
Keep the role play respectful: no shouting at or touching each other
Use markers in a ventilated room and keep the floor clear of paper
Follow the Centre's rules for the classroom
